For your 2023 GasGas MC 250F:
- **Static sag: 35 mm (1.38 in)** — bike upright under its own weight, no rider.
- **Rider sag: 105 mm (4.13 in)** — you aboard in full riding gear, feet on the pegs, with a helper balancing the bike.

Both are measured as the drop from fully extended rear suspension, using the same rear-axle-to-fender points. Set rider sag first, then check static sag: too little static sag means the shock spring is too soft; too much means it’s too stiff.
Your 2023 GasGas MC 250F targets are 35 mm static sag and 105 mm rider sag.

Honda calls for fork oil replacement every **9 races or about 22.5 riding hours**, plus **after the first break-in ride** on your 2022 CRF250R.

For hard race practice or frequent sand riding, servicing sooner—around **10–15 hours**—is common practice. Don’t wait for the interval if the fork starts leaking or its damping becomes inconsistent. Honda specifies **5W fork fluid**.

**Check fork air pressure first—don’t soften it just because it feels harsh.** Too little air lets the fork ride deep in the stroke, where small chop feels sharp, while leaving too little travel for landings.

1. **Fork air:** check cold with the front wheel off the ground. GasGas’s stock reference is **10.4 bar (151 psi)**; record your pressure before changing it. Release trapped outer-chamber air through the bleeder screws, then close them—these are separate from the spring-air valve.
2. **Only if it dives and rides deep after that:** turn fork compression **2 clicks in from its current position** for more hold-up. Stock compression and rebound are **12 clicks out**, counted from lightly seated; those are references, not a reason to reset everything together.

Does it dive and stay low under braking, or ride high and deflect over the chop? Retest the pressure correction alone over the same section before touching a clicker.

**Changes to try, one at a time:**
- **Fork spring air pressure:** Measure cold with the front wheel off the ground; use 10.4 bar (151 psi) as the stock reference if the current pressure is incorrect.
- **Fork compression—only if diving and riding deep:** From the current position, turn 2 clicks in; test only after the pressure check.
Check fork air pressure before softening compression: harshness plus bottoming can mean the fork is riding too deep, not too stiff.

Your fork needs more braking support—**check the air spring before adding damping**.

1. With the fork cold and front wheel off the ground, check its main air pressure. GASGAS’s stock reference is **10.4 bar (151 psi)**; the right pressure for you also depends on rider weight.
2. **Fork compression: turn in 2 clicks from your current position.** If you’re at the stock 12 clicks out, go from **12 to 10 clicks out**. Leave rebound unchanged. This should reduce dive without making the front deflect over braking bumps.
3. Verify rear balance: GASGAS specifies **105 mm riding sag and 35 mm static sag**. A rear sitting too high can exaggerate the nose-down feel.

Retest the same braking zone for a few laps. Return compression to its previous setting if the bars feel harsher or the front loses grip without noticeably better support.

For technique, stand and brace with your legs before squeezing the brake; keep hips over the pegs rather than pitching onto the bars. Practise five controlled straight-line stops at an easy pace.

If this started suddenly or the fork is leaking or sticking, check that fault before tuning around it.
Check the fork’s cold air pressure first, then try fork compression 2 clicks firmer to reduce brake dive.

**One click at a time** is the best testing step on your 2022 CRF250R—testers consistently find this suspension sensitive to small changes. Two clicks can make the difference easier to feel, but start with one.

- **Compression:** out makes it softer; in makes it firmer.
- **Rebound:** out makes it return faster; in makes it return slower.

Change only one adjuster, ride the same section for a few laps at a consistent pace, then compare against your original setting. If it gets worse, put it back before trying anything else. Write each setting down, counted out from lightly seated—never force the stop.

The shock’s **high-speed compression uses turns, not clicks**; keep that separate from this click-by-click test.

**Soft and bouncy after 20 minutes, but fine cold, points to shock damping fading as it heats up.** The spring hasn’t become softer—the shock is losing control of it.

Most likely, in order:
- Degraded or aerated oil: hot damping weakens, so the rear sinks more easily and rebounds faster.
- Low nitrogen charge or a leaking separator seal: lets the oil foam and damping become inconsistent. Honda specifically calls for a nitrogen-loss check if rear ride height drops after riding.
- Worn piston band or internal seals: oil bypass increases as the shock warms.

With the bike cold and securely supported, inspect the shock shaft, seal area and reservoir for oil or damage. A dry shock can still have an internal fault; have a suspension shop check nitrogen retention, oil condition and internal sealing rather than clicking around it.

How many riding hours since the shock was last serviced? **Don’t run another full moto with the rear bouncing or bottoming unpredictably.**
That points to heat-related shock damping fade, not a clicker problem. Check for leakage cold, then have the shock’s nitrogen charge and internals checked before another full moto.

Yes—the tires absorb the first part of every bump, so pressure changes can feel like suspension changes.

- **Higher pressure:** firmer, sharper impacts and more deflection, but better rim protection on rocks, square edges and hard landings.
- **Lower pressure:** more compliance and grip, but too low feels vague or squirmy and risks pinch flats and rim damage.

Honda’s cold baseline for your 2023 CRF450R is **100 kPa (15 psi) front and rear**. Set that first before chasing clickers. As general tuning practice, try about **1 psi at a time**—lower for smooth, slick ground or deep sand; higher for sharp impacts and rim protection. Leave the suspension unchanged and compare the same section.

Stop lowering pressure at the first rim strike or tire squirm. Check pressure cold at the track; don’t bleed hot tires back down to the cold baseline.

**Your shock spring is likely too soft.** You’ve needed enough preload to get the rider sag to 105 mm that the rear barely settles under the bike’s own weight.

GasGas specifies **35 mm static sag** with **105 mm rider sag**; your 20 mm static sag is 15 mm short. Assuming the linkage moves freely and the measurements repeat, that points toward a stiffer shock spring—not a clicker change.

Recheck both measurements after pushing the rear down, then after lifting it slightly and letting it settle. A large difference means friction or binding needs checking first. Don’t simply back off preload to get 35 mm static sag; that will increase rider sag beyond the target.

What do you weigh in full riding gear? That will help size the spring change.
Only 20 mm static sag with the correct 105 mm rider sag points to a shock spring that is too soft and needs excessive preload.

On your 2023 CRF450R’s **standard shock spring 56 N/mm, 222.9 mm (8.78 in) is the shortest permitted installed length**. Shorter than that is too much preload—use a firmer spring rather than winding it down further.

- Honda’s standard installed length is **232.3 mm (9.15 in)**; the permitted range is **222.9–233 mm (8.78–9.20 in)**. Measure spring seat-to-seat with the rear wheel off the ground.
- One adjuster turn shortens the spring by **1.5 mm**, adding **84 N of preload**. It raises the rear and reduces sag; it does not increase spring rate.
- Aim for **105 mm rider sag**, measured seated in normal riding position with full gear and the bike at race weight.

You can also have too much preload before reaching that length limit: if correct rider sag leaves almost no free sag, the spring is too soft. Honda does not publish a free-sag target for this bike; **30–40 mm is general tuning guidance**, measured with the bike upright and no rider.

Check installed length and both sag measurements before adding more preload.
On the stock shock spring, preload is excessive if the installed spring length is shorter than 222.9 mm, or if correct rider sag leaves almost no free sag.

Most ride-to-ride sag changes come from **measurement differences or suspension friction**. If the preload lock ring is loose, the adjustment can also move.

Your CRF250R’s standard target is **105 mm race sag with the stock shock spring 50 N/mm**. Before changing preload again:

1. Measure with the same gear, fuel load, rider position and shock temperature. Honda’s measuring points are the left rear fender bolt center and chain-adjuster locknut center; start with the rear wheel off the ground.
2. With you aboard and a helper balancing, push the rear down and let it settle; measure. Then lift it slightly and let it settle; measure again. A noticeable difference points toward linkage, swingarm or shock friction. Average the readings for a repeatable baseline.
3. Check the preload lock ring is secure and mark its position so movement is obvious. Inspect for shock leakage and bearing play; **don’t ride with loose suspension parts or a leaking shock**.

Honda publishes no static-sag target for this bike; roughly **30–40 mm is general guidance**, measured rider-off with both wheels grounded.

How many millimeters is it changing between rides? That separates measuring variation from a real change worth investigating.
Changing sag usually comes from inconsistent measuring, suspension friction, or a preload collar moving—not a spring rate changing between rides.

**Bleed them after practice and between motos**, with the front wheel off the ground and the forks fully extended. Your CRF450R has coil-spring forks—you're releasing trapped pressure, not adjusting an air spring.

1. Put the bike securely on a stand with the front wheel hanging free. Let the forks cool first.
2. Clean around the **small air-release screws at the top of both fork legs**. Don't loosen the large fork caps or the damping adjusters.
3. Slowly loosen each air-release screw just enough to let any pressure hiss out. You don't need to remove it.
4. Once the hissing stops, gently snug each screw closed—don't crank it down.

Trapped pressure can make the fork feel progressively firmer during a ride.

If you mean rebuilding the **left-hand air spring**, that is more than bleeding the fork. **Do not loosen a fork cap or open the air cartridge while pressurized**—opening the outer-chamber bleeder does not discharge the main air spring.

For routine external service:
1. With the fork cold and engine off, put the bike securely on a stand with the front wheel hanging free.
2. Loosen the small bleeder screw on each fork cap to release trapped outer-chamber pressure, then close both screws. Leave the main air valve alone for this step.
3. Remove the fork protectors, lower the dust boots, and clean behind them and along the tubes. Lightly lubricate with universal oil spray on a rag, keeping it off the brakes; reseat the boots and wipe away excess.

For internal service, the exact air-cartridge teardown, lubrication placement and inspection limits aren't confirmed here. A proper rebuild includes checking the air piston, seals, shaft and equalization passage—not simply adding oil.

**Clickers adjust the tune; a revalve changes what the suspension can be tuned to do.**

- **A revalve** changes the internal shim stacks—and sometimes pistons or bleed passages—so the tuner can reshape that response: easier movement over sharp chop, more support under braking, better landing control, or different rebound recovery. Those changes interact; a good tune balances them rather than simply making everything softer.

On your **2022 CRF250R**, testers consistently report a firm, harsh fork paired with a softer shock. A tailored revalve can address that mismatch rather than chasing comfort with clickers and losing hold-up elsewhere.

The tell is when softer compression improves chop but creates excessive dive, or firmer compression stops bottoming but beats up your hands. That's where internal tuning can do what the adjusters cannot. **Correct springs and sag come first**—a revalve doesn't replace either, and fork oil volume is a separate tool for end-stroke resistance.
Clickers fine-tune the existing damping; a revalve changes the damping curve itself, letting the suspension absorb chop without sacrificing support.

**The main difference is what holds the bike up: compressed air versus a steel coil spring.** Both use oil to control compression and rebound.

Inside your MC 250F’s WP XACT AER:
- **Air-spring leg:** a sealed piston compresses trapped air as the fork moves down. Less air space means rapidly rising pressure, so it gets progressively harder to compress near full travel. A negative-air chamber counteracts the main chamber near full extension, helping the fork start moving smoothly rather than snap against its extension stop.
- **Damping leg:** a piston pushes oil through passages, shim valves and adjustable bleed circuits. These control movement speed—not the air spring itself.

A coil fork replaces that main air-spring assembly with a steel spring, sometimes with springs in both legs depending on the design. A straight-rate coil builds force more evenly; trapped air above the oil still adds bottoming resistance.

Air saves weight and lets you change support with a pump; coils need a spring swap to change rate and are less temperature-sensitive. GasGas’s stock air setting is **10.4 bar (151 psi), checked cold**. The fork bleeder screws release outer-chamber pressure, not the main air spring.

**Compression tests show pressure built; leak-down tests show sealing loss and where it goes.**

A compression tester records pressure while the starter turns the engine. It’s a useful overall check, but battery strength, cranking speed, valve timing and automatic decompression can affect the reading. A low result alone doesn’t tell you which part is responsible.

A leak-down test feeds regulated compressed air into the cylinder with the piston at top dead center on the compression stroke, both valves closed. The tester measures leakage, and you listen for its path:
- **Intake:** intake valves leaking past their seats.
- **Exhaust:** exhaust valves leaking past their seats.
- **Crankcase breather:** leakage past the rings/piston/cylinder; some is normal.
- **Bubbles in the coolant:** possible head-gasket, head or cylinder sealing problem.

For your 450 SX-F, leak-down is especially useful before deciding whether a low compression reading means a teardown. It won’t prove valve timing or the decompression mechanism is correct, and a cold test can miss a heat-related fault.

Compressed air can turn the engine suddenly, so the crank must be secured correctly during testing.
A compression test checks how much pressure the engine builds while cranking. A leak-down test checks how well the cylinder holds pressure—and helps locate where it escapes.

**Squish is the gap between the piston’s outer edge and the matching band in the cylinder head when the piston reaches the top of its stroke.** On your YZ125, that band squeezes the fuel-air mixture inward toward the spark plug as the piston comes up.

That movement creates turbulence, helping the mixture burn faster and more consistently. Builders set the clearance to sharpen response and make combustion more efficient—not simply to raise compression.

- **Too tight:** the piston can touch the head at high rpm as parts heat, stretch and move within their bearing clearances.

A plug chop means **running at one steady throttle opening, then killing the engine without letting it idle afterward**. On your YZ125, a full-throttle chop mainly checks the main-jet circuit.

1. Warm the engine fully. Start with a clean, known-good **NGK BR9EVX**, gapped **0.6–0.7 mm (0.024–0.028 in)**.
2. On a closed course with clear runoff, accelerate in a gear that loads the engine without lugging or hitting the limiter. Hold the throttle opening you’re checking long enough for the engine to run consistently—not just a quick blip.
3. At the end of the run, **pull the clutch, press the kill button and close the throttle together**. Keep the clutch pulled and coast to a safe stop. Don’t restart or idle back.
4. Let the engine cool, clean dirt away from the plug, then remove it. Dry soot suggests richness; a wet plug can mean fouling or misfire. Blistering, melted electrodes or metallic specks are danger signs—not a cue for another test.

General practice: don’t choose jets from insulator color alone; fuel, oil and previous running affect it. Stop immediately for pinging or surging. Refit the plug by hand first, then torque to **20 Nm (15 ft-lb)**.
A plug chop captures the plug’s condition at one throttle opening by stopping combustion before idling changes the reading. Test under load on a closed course with a clear coast-down area.

**Final-drive ratio = rear sprocket teeth ÷ front sprocket teeth.**

Your 2022 CRF250R’s stock gearing is **13 front / 50 rear**:
**50 ÷ 13 = 3.846**, usually written **3.85:1**. The front sprocket turns about 3.85 times for each rear-wheel revolution.

- **Higher number = shorter gearing:** stronger pull, less speed at the same engine rpm in the same gear.
- **Lower number = taller gearing:** longer gears, more speed at the same rpm, but less pull.

For example, 13/51 gives **3.923:1**—a **2% shorter** ratio than stock. To compare any change: **(new ratio ÷ old ratio − 1) × 100**.

That’s the sprocket ratio only; overall engine-to-wheel gearing also includes the primary drive and whichever transmission gear you’re using.

A too-tight chain doesn’t just wear faster—it can **fight the rear suspension and overload the bearings**.

The front sprocket isn’t centered on the swingarm pivot, so the distance between sprockets changes as the swingarm moves. The chain is tightest when the countershaft, swingarm pivot and rear axle line up. Set it too tight with the suspension extended, and it can run out of slack before reaching that point.

That puts heavy loads into the countershaft and rear-wheel bearings, chain and sprockets. It also resists suspension movement, making the rear feel harsh and lose traction. In extreme cases, the chain or another drivetrain component can fail.

For your **2023 450 SX-F**, KTM’s check is with the engine off and rear wheel hanging free: pull the upper chain run upward at the rear end of the chain slider, keeping the lower run taut, and measure the gap: **58–61 mm (2.28–2.4 in)**. Rotate the wheel and check several positions—tight spots matter. This is that specific gap measurement, not total up-and-down chain movement.

If it’s too tight, adjust it before riding.
